title: Half-Life Clocks in Rocks
learningObjectives: Define half-life as the time required for one-half of parent atoms to decay to daughter atoms.
Calculate remaining parent amount from starting amount, half-life, and elapsed time using exponential decay.
Explain how measurements of remaining parent and new daughter atoms are used to compute the numeric age of a rock.

evidence.quote: The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the length of time required for exactly one-half of the parent atoms to decay to daughter atoms.
The change from parent to daughter happens at a constant rate, called the half-life.

explanations.text: Half-life is the constant-rate time needed for exactly half of parent atoms to decay to daughter atoms.

evidence.quote: A radioactive isotope (the parent) of one chemical element naturally converts to a stable isotope
are used to compute the age of the rock.

explanations.text: A parent isotope converts in the nucleus to a stable daughter isotope, and remaining and new atoms are used to compute rock age.

evidence.quote: Each radioactive isotope has its own unique half-life.
four parent/daughter decay series are especially useful: carbon to nitrogen, potassium to argon, rubidium to strontium, and uranium to lead.

explanations.text: Each isotope has its own half-life, and series such as carbon to nitrogen and uranium to lead are useful for dating geologic materials.
